messages.author: e3cd7ac95409208e
messages.subject: Plot high dimensional (factors >3) models?
parts:
Just fishing around for suggestions to plot item characteristic curves (or something similar) when I have 5 (or more) latent variables? Is there some type of contour-like plot (which I know only works for 2 dimensions) that people may be familiar with?

Or would the recommended practice would be to fit several unidimensional models and explore things visually at that level?

Thank you!

Elia

messages.author: b330c2028fed415b
messages.subject: Re: Plot high dimensional (factors >3) models?
parts:
Five dimensions is pretty hard to interpret regardless of the type of plot selected. I'm assuming this is an exploratory IRT model. If so, I think you should care more about rotation after convergence (via summary()) than plotting so that future confirmatory models can be fitted that are easier to interpret. 

Phil

Thank you!

Thank you, Phil! You are correct. This is, indeed, an exploratory-type model. I was feeling optimistic because, as surprising as it may sound, it's yielding good fit at a somewhat large sample (N>2000) with stuff consistent with the general theory from where the scale was developed. 

But thank you for your suggestion, I will concentrate on the rotation used. Is there any particular type of (oblique) rotation that you might have seen perform well with high-dimensional models? I can see the default is "oblimin" in mirt but I can see Mplus uses "geomin", of instance.

messages.author: b330c2028fed415b
messages.subject: Re: Plot high dimensional (factors >3) models?
parts:
On Wed, Aug 24, 2016 at 1:51 PM, Elia Emmers <eliae...@gmail.com> wrote:
Thank you, Phil! You are correct. This is, indeed, an exploratory-type model. I was feeling optimistic because, as surprising as it may sound, it's yielding good fit at a somewhat large sample (N>2000) with stuff consistent with the general theory from where the scale was developed.
Glad to hear it; sounds like you are on the road to finding something publishable.

But thank you for your suggestion, I will concentrate on the rotation used. Is there any particular type of (oblique) rotation that you might have seen perform well with high-dimensional models? I can see the default is "oblimin" in mirt but I can see Mplus uses "geomin", of instance.

I don't think it really matters all that much, and I certainly am not in any camp on which is best; I always use the oblimin default since I'm sure it's good enough. Just use whichever one simplifies the structure best and lines up best with your theory (this is exploratory after all). I do however believe that you should always use oblique rotations because traits are more likely to be correlated than not (so things like varimax are probably not the best). Cheers.

Phil

messages.author: b330c2028fed415b
messages.subject: Re: Plot high dimensional (factors >3) models?
parts: On Sun, Sep 25, 2016 at 4:03 AM, Oce <oce....@gmail.com> wrote:
Thanks a lot Phil, I tried drop.zeros but its 3D representation made it very difficult to visualize....
I am currently doing this:

itemplot(Bf.data.2, 1, drop.zeros= T, rot=list(xaxis = 0, yaxis=90, zaxis = 90), theta_lim = c(0,6))

which is more 2D like and can show what the plot looks like when theta is 0....
I am wondering if this is appropriate, or if there is a more proper way of showing a real 2D graph...

It's not really appropriate, it's just cutting off a lot of the plot range. Perhaps try presenting faceted plots of slices along the general factor. 

library(mirt)
data(SAT12)
data <- key2binary(SAT12,
  key = c(1,4,5,2,3,1,2,1,3,1,2,4,2,1,5,3,4,4,1,4,3,3,4,1,3,5,1,3,1,5,4,5))
specific <- c(2,3,2,3,3,2,1,2,1,1,1,3,1,3,1,2,1,1,3,3,1,1,3,1,3,3,1,3,2,3,1,2)
mod1 <- bfactor(data, specific, TOL = NA)
itemplot(mod1, 1, drop.zeros = TRUE)

Theta <- seq(-4, 4, length.out = 100)
Theta <- cbind(Theta, Theta, Theta)
Theta_outer <- -4:4

i1 <- extract.item(mod1, 1)
ps <- vector('list', length(Theta_outer))
count <- 1
for(i in Theta_outer){
ps[[count]] <- probtrace(i1, cbind(i, Theta))[,2]
count <- count + 1
}

par(mfrow = c(3,3))
for(i in 1:length(ps))
plot(Theta[,1], ps[[i]], main = paste0('General Factor = ', Theta_outer[i]), type = 'l',
xlab = expression(theta), ylab = expression(P(theta)))

Have you tried using the drop.zeros option in itemplot? That may be more helpful for presenting the model item by item to those less familiar with higher dimensional models. Cheers.

Phil
